questions.q: Why can an unconstrained decision tree be especially dangerous on financial data?
options: Decision trees cannot handle numeric features
An unconstrained tree can grow until it memorizes the training data almost perfectly, including noise -- a serious risk when real signal explains only 1-2% of variance
Trees require data to be standardized first
Decision trees cannot be used for regression
questions.explain: Left unconstrained, a tree can split until leaves contain just a few samples, fitting noise as well as signal -- especially damaging when the real signal is already faint.

questions.q: Which two parameters are the primary overfitting controls for a `DecisionTreeRegressor`?
options: learning_rate and n_estimators
max_depth and min_samples_leaf
alpha and l1_ratio
C and kernel
questions.explain: Limiting max_depth (how deep the tree can grow) and min_samples_leaf (how few samples a leaf can have) are the standard controls against overfitting in a single tree.

questions.q: How does a random forest reduce the overfitting risk of a single decision tree?
options: By using only one very deep tree
By training many trees on bootstrapped rows and random feature subsets, then averaging their predictions so each tree's distinct noise cancels out
By removing all regularization
By converting the problem into classification
questions.explain: Because each tree overfits to different noise (due to bootstrapping and random feature subsets), averaging many trees cancels much of that noise while real shared signal survives.

questions.q: In scikit-learn, which attribute of a fitted RandomForestRegressor gives a first look at which features drove predictions?
options: .coef_
.feature_importances_
.support_
.explained_variance_
questions.explain: `.feature_importances_` reports how much each feature contributed to reducing error across the forest's trees -- a useful but imperfect first look, refined in Chapter 5.

questions.q: Why does this lesson describe `.feature_importances_` as a 'rough first look, not a final answer'?
options: Because it is always exactly correct

Because the default importance measure has real limitations (such as bias toward high-cardinality features), and more robust methods like permutation importance and SHAP are covered later in Chapter 5
Because it only works with linear models
Because it cannot be computed for more than 10 features
questions.explain: Default feature importances can be biased and are a starting point only -- Chapter 5 introduces permutation importance and SHAP as more rigorous alternatives.
